Empirical Research Plan  
“Compulsory Schooling Laws, Schooling Attainment, and Human-Capital Externalities”

------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
------------------------------------------------------------------
Primary strategy: Staggered Difference-in-Differences (DID) combined with an Instrumental-Variables (2SLS) framework.

• First stage (policy → schooling):  
   Exploit state-by-cohort variation in the minimum school-leaving age (MSLA) created by compulsory-schooling-law (CSL) changes.  

• Second stage (schooling → outcomes, incl. externalities):  
   Instrument individual schooling (or average schooling in a local labor-market cell) with the interaction of birth cohort and state MSLA status.  

Why appropriate?  
– CSL reforms are plausibly exogenous to individual characteristics, but they affect actual years of schooling strongly (high first-stage F-stats in the literature).  
– Staggered adoption across states and over time delivers clean within-state-over-time contrasts (DID).  
– IV is required because schooling is endogenously chosen; CSLs supply the exogenous variation needed to identify causal effects on earnings and on externalities (e.g., effect of peers’ schooling on own earnings).

------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control Definition  
------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
  Treatist = 1 if individual i is in birth cohort c in state s such that compulsory-schooling age in state s at the time cohort c turned the original leaving age was raised by ≥ 1 year (i.e., binding reform). Otherwise 0.

Control group  
  1. Same-state cohorts born just before the reform (not subject to new MSLA).  
  2. Same-cohort individuals in states that did not change their CSL in that year.  
This delivers the classical DID 2×2 comparison but extended to multiple reforms (Goodman-Bacon decomposition).

Treatment timing / event date  
  For state s, ReformYear_s is the first school year in which the higher MSLA applied. Individuals born ≥ ReformYear_s – (OriginalLeavingAge+1) are “treated”.

(No RDD running variable is used.)

------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel Trends (DID): Absent the CSL change, outcomes of treated and control groups would have followed parallel trends.  
  Plausibility: School-leaving laws were often changed for nationwide child-labor or military-preparedness motives, not state-specific earnings trends. Event-study graphs help assess this.

A2. Relevance (IV): CSL reforms must increase schooling.  
  Plausibility: Historical evidence shows 0.10–0.40 additional years of schooling per extra year of mandated schooling.

A3. Exclusion (IV): CSL affects earnings (own or others’) only through schooling, not through other channels.  
  Plausibility: CSLs do not directly change tax policy or labor-demand conditions; remaining concerns handled with controls for contemporaneous child-labor laws and industrialization.

A4. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no cross-state anticipation spillovers within estimation window).  
  Plausibility: Families seldom migrated solely to avoid one extra year of school; we test by excluding highly mobile groups.

------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigation  
------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Policy endogeneity to economic conditions (states raise MSLA in downturns).  
   Mitigation: Include state-specific linear and quadratic trends, pre-reform macro controls, and drop reforms enacted during severe, state-specific shocks as robustness.

T2. Selective migration of families around school-leaving cutoffs.  
   Mitigation: (i) Control for state of birth (not residence) when available; (ii) show results hold when restricting to low-mobility sub-samples (e.g., non-movers until age 18).

T3. Contemporaneous policy bundles (child-labor restrictions, school funding).  
   Mitigation: Add controls for child-labor-law stringency, teacher-pupil ratios, and state education expenditures; run a triple-diff dropping states that simultaneously changed these.

------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline (executable)  
------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # data wrangling
library(fixest)       # fast high-dimensional FE, IV
library(ggplot2)      # plots
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load and merge data
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
census <- fread("census_individuals.csv")        # individual micro data
laws   <- fread("csl_state_year.csv")            # compulsory schooling law panel
mob    <- fread("migration_controls.csv")        # mobility, other policy controls

# merge law info
setkey(census, state, birth_year)
setkey(laws,   state, cohort_year)
dat <- laws[census, roll = TRUE]   # assigns CSL in force when cohort hits leaving age
dat <- merge(dat, mob, by = c("state","year"), all.x = TRUE)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Construct variables
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# schooling
dat[, yrs_school := educ_years]

# treatment indicator = 1 if new MSLA exceeds old and cohort is binding
dat[, treat := as.integer(msla_new > msla_old & exposed == 1)]

# average schooling in local labor market (state x birth cohort) – for externality
dat[, avg_school_statecohort := mean(yrs_school), by = .(state, birth_year)]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main 2SLS specification
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# First stage: schooling on treatment
fs <- feols(yrs_school ~ treat | state + birth_year, data = dat,
            cluster = ~state)
summary(fs)

# Second stage: own earnings
iv_own <- feols(log(earnings) ~ 1 | state + birth_year | (yrs_school ~ treat),
                cluster = ~state, data = dat)
summary(iv_own)

# Externality: effect of avg schooling of peers on individual earnings
# instrumented with leave-one-out predicted schooling
dat[, peer_school := avg_school_statecohort - yrs_school/.N]  # leave-one-out
iv_ext <- feols(log(earnings) ~ 1 | state + birth_year | (peer_school ~ treat),
                cluster = ~state, data = dat)
summary(iv_ext)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Robustness: event-study (pre-trends)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
dat[, rel_year := birth_year - reform_cohort]      # years relative to reform
# keep ±10 window
es <- feols(log(earnings) ~ i(rel_year, ref = -1) |
            state + birth_year ,                  # two-way FE
            cluster = ~state, data = dat[abs(rel_year)<=10])
iplot(es) + ggtitle("Event-study plot: log earnings around CSL reform")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
```

------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results (prior)  
------------------------------------------------------------------
• Direct return to schooling (own earnings): +8–10 percent per additional year.  
• Externality: A 1-year increase in average schooling of peers in the same state-cohort raises an individual’s earnings by ≈ 1–2 percent (positive spillover through productivity and knowledge diffusion).

------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID + IV)  
(1 = clearly satisfied; 0 = questionable)  
------------------------------------------------------------------
C1 (Parallel trends validated via pre-trends tests) ………………… 0.8  
C2 (Strong first-stage relevance, F > 10) …………………………… 1.0  
C3 (Exclusion restriction plausible, no direct policy channels) … 0.6  
C4 (No selective migration around reform) ………………………… 0.7  
C5 (SUTVA: limited interference across states/cohorts) ………… 0.8  

Average score ≈ 0.78 → Decent but not bulletproof; robustness checks essential.

------------------------------------------------------------------
This plan delivers a rigorous causal estimate of both private and social returns to education induced by compulsory-schooling reforms.
